newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-EU pledges gene-modified food policy review.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU pledges gene-modified food policy review.

text.p: The European Commission, aware of consumer unease in the wake of the mad-cow-disease beef scare in Europe, pledged on Wednesday to review the way the EU clears gene-modified products.
Commission President Jacques Santer made the pledge during the EU executive's weekly meeting after talks on approval procedures for Ciba Geigy's gene-modified maize.

"The president at the end of the debate over maize underlined that, as shown by the other public discussion over soyabeans, genetically modified products pose a problem with public opinion," said spokesman Nikolaus van der Pas.

The EU has already approved several gene-modified products for sale in the 15-country bloc, including U.S. chemical company Monsanto's Round Up Ready soyabeans, which have been altered to resist one of the company's weedkillers.

Recent U.S.-origin shipments of soyabeans, thought to contain some gene-modified beans from this year's harvest, have sparked direct-action protests by environmentalists and verbal complaints from European consumer organisations and retailers who want to be able to tell customers which products contain derivatives from gene-modified beans.

European Union approval for Swiss company Ciba's gene-modified corn has been held up repeatedly amid concerns about its safety, with many of the EU's environment ministers saying they were against approval at a meeting last June.

"To prevent such a problem arising each time, we are going to start at zero. The president has concluded that the Commission should soon have a debate to see how the problem that now exists can be resolved," van der Pas told a news conference.
European Environment Commissioner Ritt Bjerrregaard told a Strasbourg news conference that three EU scientific committees looking into the maize question had yet to reach a decision.
"We are waiting for them to respond -- it's too early to say what happens if they agree or (do not) agree...we will simply have to wait and see," she said.
But an American agricultural official said that gene-modified organisms were nothing new in Europe and that the debate should not focus on U.S. soyabeans.
"Biotechnology is not that new in Europe," George Pope, U.S. agricultural attache in Brussels told a grains conference held by the Agra Europe consultancy and newsletter publisher.
He said that European butter and cheese was probably produced with gene-modified enzymes, bread and cake contained gene-modified yeast and some meat was also gene-modified.
Cigarette smokers also had to be careful because gene-modified tobacco was being grown in Europe.
"Most pharmaceutical products today are made through genetic modification," he said.
Pope added that shoppers were unlikely to find a special label on any of these products and were thus unable to make a choice.

European consumer distrust, both about food safety and the authority of food scientists' recommendations, has grown this year in the wake of findings showing a possible link between Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), the fatal brain-wasting disease in cattle, and its human equivalent in people who have eaten infected beef.

The Union has been criticised by its own biotechnology industry for an approval procedure which takes far longer than in the United States and other countries, an issue partly due to the widely divergent positions on the use of genetically modified organisms (GMOs) among and within EU countries.
